topic: World History Topics (two, same as SL)
subject: history

items.title: The First Crusade captured Jerusalem with massacre in 1099
items.claim: What happened when the First Crusade took Jerusalem?

options.text: On 15 July 1099 crusaders breached the walls; over the following days a massacre of Muslim and Jewish inhabitants followed — chroniclers (including Raymond of Aguilers) recorded slaughter so extensive that 'one waded in blood up to the ankles'

items.reveal:
The crusade had left Europe in 1096. After taking Antioch (1098), the army of around 14,000 reached Jerusalem in June 1099. The walls were breached on 15 July; the massacre that followed killed thousands. Jewish inhabitants who took refuge in a synagogue were burned alive.

Godfrey of Bouillon was elected 'Defender of the Holy Sepulchre' (refusing the title of king); his brother Baldwin became Baldwin I of Jerusalem in 1100. The Kingdom of Jerusalem lasted until 1291 (fall of Acre).

Saladin recaptured Jerusalem in 1187 with notably less violence — he allowed inhabitants to ransom themselves and many to leave safely, in deliberate contrast to 1099.
items.why: Religious warfare in the high Middle Ages was often atrocious. The 1099 massacre shaped Muslim-Christian relations for centuries — and the comparison with Saladin's 1187 conduct is one that Muslim sources have made repeatedly.

items.title: Around 50,000 Huguenots fled to England in the 1680s
items.claim: Why did French Huguenots come to England?

options.text: They were invited as agricultural labour by William III
Louis XIV revoked the Edict of Nantes (1598) in 1685, removing Protestant rights — around 50,000 fled to England, with major settlements in Spitalfields, Soho and Canterbury
They were exiled by James II for Jacobite sympathies
Famine in Brittany drove migration in the 1680s

items.reveal:
The Revocation of the Edict of Nantes (October 1685) made Protestant worship illegal in France. Perhaps 200,000-400,000 Huguenots fled total — to England, the Dutch Republic, Brandenburg, the Cape and the American colonies.

In England they brought silk-weaving (Spitalfields), gunmaking, watchmaking, banking (the Courtauld and Bosanquet families). 'Refugee' as an English word enters the language from the Huguenot experience.

Charles II had already extended denizenship to French Protestants in 1681. Anti-Catholic sentiment made absorption relatively smooth.
items.why: Migration history in Britain is much older than the 20th century. The Huguenot case is the classic example of refugees whose skills shaped an industrial sector — and whose absorption was made easier by religious alignment.

items.title: McCarthy was censured by his own Senate in 1954
items.claim: How did Joseph McCarthy's anti-communist campaign end?

options.text: After televised Army-McCarthy hearings exposed his methods, the Senate voted 67-22 to censure him on 2 December 1954; he died of liver failure in 1957 aged 48
He resigned and joined the Republican Party leadership

items.reveal:
McCarthy had risen on a 1950 Wheeling speech claiming 205 communists in the State Department. The Army-McCarthy hearings (April-June 1954) were televised; Army counsel Joseph Welch's 'Have you no sense of decency, sir?' on 9 June became the iconic moment.

Edward R. Murrow's CBS broadcast 'See It Now' on 9 March 1954 had already turned mainstream opinion. The Senate censure vote followed in December.

HUAC (House Un-American Activities Committee), the Hollywood blacklist, loyalty oaths and the Smith Act prosecutions continued separately and outlasted McCarthy.
items.why: McCarthyism as a phenomenon was bigger than McCarthy. His fall did not end the Red Scare — but it ended one specific style of grandstanding accusation, and television was central to both his rise and fall.
